# Mobile cognitive remote assessment of schizophrenia: a global multi-site pilot study

Juan Castillo1,6, Jiaee Cheong1,6, Soumya Choudhary2, Ameya Bondre 3, Abhijit R. Rozatkar 4, Urvakhsh Meherwan Mehta 2, Ritu Shrivastava3, Manaal Amir Ahmad3, Anshika Malviya3, Yogendra Sen3, Deepak Tugnawat3, Anant Bhan3, Tamonud Modak4, Nabagata Das 2, Srilakshmi Nagendra2, Preethi Reddy 3, Ronak Chatterjee 4, Erlend Lane1, John A. Naslund5 and John Torous 1✉

Cognition in schizophrenia is difﬁcult to assess in clinical settings due to the time required to administer traditional pen-and-paper tests, among other factors. Digital remote assessments completed on a smartphone offer an alternative that can reduce the burden on healthcare staff and patients, in addition to providing more nuanced cognitive proﬁles, especially when used in conjunction with smartphone data such as sleep. Building on previous work using the mindLAMP research app in international contexts, this paper presents a global multi-site pilot study to explore the validity of the app’s digital cognitive assessments as proxies for traditional in-person assessments such as the gold standard MATRICS Consensus Battery (MCCB). Across one site in the U.S. (Boston) and two sites in India (Bangalore and Bhopal), a total of 56 participants with diagnoses of early-course schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder were recruited between September 2024 and March 2025 to engage with the mindLAMP app for 30 days. Participants completed 2-3 different cognitive tasks and surveys each day; at the beginning and the end of this period, participants also took the MCCB and surveys related to their diagnosis. mindLAMP cognitive assessments were scored using different metrics that combine speed and accuracy, and correlation analyses were run on these metrics and MCCB domains. Of the scoring metrics used, the Rate-Correct Score (RCS) most consistently correlates with baseline MCCB domains corrected for age, gender, and education. Moderate test-retest reliability was observed across certain cognitive assessments such as a mobile version of Trails- Making Test A and Symbol Digit Substitution, which agrees with previous research done by Keefe et al.; poor test-retest reliability, in contrast, was observed across assessments such as Spatial Span. Additionally, we conducted exploratory mediation analyses using sleep data to see if sleep mediates between the Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) survey scores and performance on select digital cognitive assessments on mindLAMP. Our results support the initial accessibility, validity and reliability of using smartphones to assess cognition in schizophrenia. Future research to develop additional smartphone-based cognitive tests, as well as with larger samples and in other psychiatric populations, is warranted.

INTRODUCTION Schizophrenia is a chronic and disabling psychiatric disorder characterized by disturbances in thought, perception, emotion, and behavior1,2. Schizophrenia hzxxxxxxxxxxxas been posited to lead to cognitive impairments in several domains such as attention, memory, and visuospatial skills3–5. Despite decades of research, effective long-term management remains a challenge due to its heterogeneous nature and the variability in symptom presentation across individuals and contexts. Traditionally, clinical assessment of schizophrenia relies on infrequent, subjective evaluations conducted in clinical settings1,2. These assessments, while important, may fail to capture the dynamic ﬂuctuations in cognitive impairment that occur in patients’ daily lives6–8. In recent years, digital remote assessments offered on smartphones and computers have emerged as promising tools to address the limitations of traditional in-person cognitive tests9–11. Within schizophrenia research, digital remote assessments have been proposed as a means to enable the recruitment of larger and more diverse samples (e.g. from rural and remote areas) and of individuals who might have logistical (e.g. cost, transportation, availability of clinicians) or symptomatic (e.g. social

avoidance or paranoia) issues that make in-person attendance difﬁcult10,12–14. Moreover, given that digital or smartphone-based assessment can be completed anytime and anywhere, such technology supports the advancement of brief assessments of cognition, otherwise known as ecological momentary assessments (EMAs)15,16. In the context of schizophrenia, where symptom expression is heterogeneous, multidimensional, and temporally dynamic, smartphone-based surveys and sensors offer an ecologically valid alternative to traditional cross-sectional neuropsychological assessments17–20. Existing works have explored and demonstrated the preliminary utility of using remote cognitive assessment as a tool for research18,21–23. NeuroUX has shown, for instance, with a healthy general adult population that remote cognitive assessments exhibit acceptable test-retest reliability and that factors such as the individual’s age and testing environment impact their performance24,25. Although there are other apps in this space24,26,27, our work focuses on using the mindLAMP as it offers a robust and extensible framework for integrating cognitive assessments and smartphone sensor data while also supporting care delivery22,28,29. mindLAMP cognitive assessments have been

studied in schizophrenia9,30,31, Parkinson’s Disease32, mild/moderate cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer’s Disease19. Given the relative nascency of this ﬁeld, there is no predetermined or gold-standard manner to evaluate these digital cognitive assessments10,33. Whereas traditional assessments such as the MCCB tend to rely on either speed (e.g. the Trails-Making Tests)34 or accuracy (e.g. BACS Symbol Coding)35 to score tasks, digital cognitive assessments have access to more speciﬁc and precise item-level data; mindLAMP, in particular, stores metadata such as duration for each user event, which generally constitutes a tap on the phone screen. Within the existing literature, digital cognitive assessments are typically scored using quantitative performance metrics that map onto well-deﬁned cognitive constructs, such as memory, attention, and processing speed10,33,36. Most research has primarily focused on time-based or accuracy-based metrics. Within the time-based scoring paradigm, scores typically correspond to time34,37,38. Some examples include total completion time4, response time, and interresponse time (IRT) or latency38. Other works rely on accuracy-based metrics where the scores are determined by the rate of correct responses and are often directly mapped to standard neuropsychological outcomes (e.g. number of correct matches in a symbol substitution task)39. However, existing work has shown that different scoring methods can yield signiﬁcantly different results and outcomes10. A key gap in the literature is that none of the existing works have investigated composite-based metrics, which combine both speed and accuracy, to score digital cognitive assessments. Our work presents the ﬁrst attempt to use a composite metric, the Rate-Correct Score (RCS), to score these assessments. Currently, there is a lack of substantial research on the correlation between digital cognitive assessments and traditional in-person MCCB tests, or with affective states as measured using established clinical scales, such as the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Building on the previous work conducted by Raje et al. which explores patient and clinician co-design of the cognitive assessments18, this study presents a global multisite pilot study of smartphone data in schizophrenia, drawing on data collected across geographically and culturally diverse regions3,22,40. This study aims to determine which metric is best suited to score the digital cognitive assessments and which cognitive assessments of the mindLAMP smartphone app may merit further study. The principal hypothesis of this paper is that scoring digital cognitive assessments as the number of correct responses per unit time will offer strong and signiﬁcant correlations with MCCB scores. In our work, we have opted to use composite metrics, which account for both accuracy and time, as research has indicated that ﬁndings are stronger for composite scores10,41.

Participants were assigned one or two cognitive assessments per day, so that they were expected to have completed each cognitive evaluation at least 4 times by the end of the study. The schedule for participants in Boston is shown in Table 3; the schedule for participants in India similarly has participants complete one or two assessments per day.

Correlations between MCCB domains and mindLAMP cognitive assessment scores Table 4 presents correlations Bonferroni-corrected for multiple comparisons between baseline MCCB domain scores and baseline scoring metrics for the mindLAMP cognitive assessments. Of the ﬁve different scoring metrics outlined in Section "Digital Cognitive Assessment Scoring Methods", the Rate-Correct Score has the strongest and most signiﬁcant correlations with baseline MCCB domain scores corrected for age, gender, and education. Importantly, the Rate-Correct Score for Jewels A correlates with both the Overall Composite Score (r = 0.597, p < 0.001) and the Overall Neurocognitive Composite Scores (r = 0.537, p < 0.001). The Rate-Correct Score for Jewels A also correlates with Speed of Processing (r = 0.464, p < 0.05), as well as Working Memory (r = 0.454, p < 0.05). The Rate-Correct Score for Symbol Digit Substitution correlates with both the Overall Composite Score (r = 0.532, p < 0.01) and the Neurocognitive Composite Scores (r = 0.530, p < 0.01), and with Working Memory (r = 0.502, p < 0.05). The alternate score for Spatial Span, which is the number of correct responses, correlates with Attention/Vigilance (r = 0.534, p < 0.01), Overall Composite Score (r = 0.505, p < 0.01), Speed of Processing (r = 0.499, p < 0.01), and the Neurocognitive

Composite Score (r = 0.449, p < 0.05). Correlations between the mindLAMP assessments and the individual subtests of the MCCB can be found in Appendix B.

Intraclass Correlation Coefﬁcients (ICCs) for mindLAMP cognitive assessments Table 5 presents ICCs for the mindLAMP digital cognitive assessments to assess test-retest reliability. Given that test-retest reliability refers to the consistency of a test or measure over time, within the context of traditional tests such as the MCCB, high reliability ensures that baseline and follow-up comparisons are meaningful42. As shown in Table 5, Balloon Risk (ICC = 0.664, 95% CI [0.570–0.764]), Jewels A (ICC = 0.568, 95% CI [0.466−0.684]), and Symbol Digit Substitution (ICC = 0.536, 95% CI [0.438−0.651]) exhibited moderate test-retest reliability. In contrast, the rest of the assessments did not demonstrate acceptable test-retest reliability. This may be due to external factors, which will be further discussed within the discussion section. By way of comparison, for a neuroUX study with 393 adults who completed each of the platform’s digital cognitive assessments ﬁve times over the course of ten days, the ICCs ranged from 0.438 for a task testing visual working memory and processing speed to 0.912 for a task testing processing speed24.

Mediation analysis Using the data from the two sites in India, we performed an exploratory analysis to see whether sleep duration calculated from mindLAMP smartphone data mediates between mindLAMP survey scores for mood and anxiety and the Rate-Correct Scores for Jewels A and Jewels B. Intraindividual z scores (i.e. distance from the mean in units of standard deviation calculated based on each participant’s distribution of data) were used for sleep, survey scores, and the Rate-Correct Scores. Given the small sample size, this analysis is primarily intended to suggest a future direction of interest for later studies.

Anxiety EMA. Figure 1 visualizes the mediation diagrams with the anxiety EMA scores as the predictor. For Jewels A, none of the indirect (r = 0.026, p > 0.05), direct (r = 0.107, p > 0.05), or total (r = 0.133, p > 0.05) effects were signiﬁcant, so that sleep did not appear to be a mediator. For Jewels B, none of the indirect (r = 0.012, p > 0.05), direct (r = 0.019, p > 0.05), or total (r = 0.031, p > 0.05) effects were signiﬁcant. Sleep was, however, almost a moderator (r = −0.18, p = 0.054).

Mood EMA. Figure 2 visualizes the mediation diagrams with the mood EMA scores as the predictor. For Jewels A, the indirect effect (r = 0.020, p > 0.05) was insigniﬁcant, but the direct (r = 0.203, p < 0.05) and total (r = 0.223, p < 0.05) effects were signiﬁcant. For Jewels B, none of the indirect (r = 0.004, p > 0.05), direct (r = 0.079, p > 0.05), or total (r = 0.083, p > 0.05) effects were signiﬁcant; however, sleep did appear to be a moderator (r = −0.214, p = 0.05).

in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia, this study aimed to determine which cognitive assessments of the mindLAMP smartphone app may merit further study. The results presented suggest the following two key ﬁndings: ﬁrst, the Rate-Correct Score43 correlates the most with scores on the MCCB; second, of the various mindLAMP cognitive assessments, Jewels A and Symbol Digit Substitution have the strongest correlational evidence with MCCB measures of both domain-speciﬁc and overall cognition. The Rate-Correct Score succinctly balances trade-offs in speed and accuracy43, two fundamental aspects of performance, by considering the number of correct responses per unit time: accuracy in isolation may be misleading if the time taken to complete a test is excessive; likewise, rapid completion of a test is unimpressive if the responses are incorrect. In this vein, it is worth noting that the Rate-Correct Score generally outperformed traditional scoring metrics based on accuracy or speed for relevant digital cognitive assessments such as Jewels A/B and Symbol Digit Substitution; traditional scoring metrics only appeared relevant for Spatial Span. This highlights the general importance of both speed and accuracy to properly scoring digital cognitive assessments, even if they were not for their traditional counterparts such as the Trails-Making Tests and BACS Symbol Coding. As highlighted in the introduction, prior mobile app cognitive assessment research16,37,39 did not use composite-based metrics to score assessments, which may limit their real-world

ecological validity and hinder research progress within the ﬁeld. Nonetheless, for some cognitive assessments, speed and accuracy can be irrelevant by design: for instance, a mobile version of the Iowa Gambling Task, which assesses risk-taking behaviour and requires users to maximize their score by preferentially selecting buttons that are more likely to award rather than detract points, does not concern itself directly with speed or accuracy, but rather with a sort of pattern recognition. Such digital cognitive assessments, however, do not correspond to the cognitive domains under consideration in the current analysis. In comparison with prior works, with respect to Intraclass Correlation Coefﬁcient (ICC) analysis, our results are comparable with and complement the ﬁndings of Keefe et al.44,45 which showed that the composite scores have high test-retest reliability. By way of comparison, Keefe et al. (2011) showed that, for a population of 323 individuals with schizophrenia, the MCCB composite score had an ICC of 0.88, and Speed of Processing had the highest ICC of 0.79, and Verbal Learning the lowest one of 0.5846. For digital cognitive assessments, environmental variability such as distractions and fatigue can introduce noise. Moreover, the test-retest reliability may also be more sensitive to mood, motivation, or even phone performance. In the paper by Shvetz et al., the authors investigated the initial accessibility, validity and reliability of using the Jewels Trails Test by comparing whether individuals with schizophrenia had signiﬁcantly lower performance compared to controls on both the in-lab Jewels Trails Test and Trails-Making Test16. Although the ﬁndings indicate promising validity, the authors have also highlighted that remote cognitive tests such as the Jewels A and B, mobile versions of the Trails-Making Tests, remain to be validated to assess actual cognitive impairments in schizophrenia, which is precisely what our study attempts to address. Moreover, the ﬁndings here complement recent studies investigating the validity of remote administration of the MCCB test47, which suggests that remote administration of some of the MCCB subtests may be a valid alternative to in-person testing. However, further research is necessary to determine why some tasks were comparatively more affected by administration format48. By integrating cognitive assessments and smartphone sensor data across multiple sites, this study offers a comprehensive examination of how smartphone data can support scalable, global mental health research. smartphone-based cognitive assessments can serve as a generalizable tool in the evaluation of cognition across a range of neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions. Cognitive decline is often subtle and difﬁcult to detect in its early stages, particularly in disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, or mild cognitive impairment5,49. By ﬁrst validating these methods in a population where cognitive dysfunction is prominent and measurable4,50 and providing promising exploratory mediation analysis on how smartphone data such as sleep mediates between performance on digital cognitive assessments and EMA survey scores, we lay the groundwork for extending this approach to other EMA use cases and populations where early and continuous cognitive monitoring may be even more critical. Moreover, as our experiments relied on EMA-based methods, the results might have greater ecological validity. In traditional neuropsychological testing, like the MCCB, participants complete tasks in lab settings with minimal real-world distractions. Such tasks may boast high construct validity51 (i.e., the test measures what it is designed to measure), but suffer from low ecological validity42 (i.e., the test does not reﬂect real-world performance and behaviour)52. This work, therefore, not only advances digital mental health for schizophrenia but also contributes a scalable, ﬂexible framework for digital cognitive assessment across the diagnostic spectrum and across an individual’s lifespan. Exploratory mediation analysis looking at whether sleep mediates between the Rate-Correct Scores for Jewels A and Jewels B on mindLAMP and EMA survey scores for mood and anxiety suggests that sleep may, in fact, be a moderator. Limitations of this work concern its generalizability given our relatively small total sample size of 56. The remote digital cognitive assessments were each done once weekly, which may

limit the reliability or validity of our results. Nonetheless, we wish to emphasize that, given reliability (in classical test theory) is a function of variation in the population under study and the precision of the test, our efforts are a step forward in that direction by collecting, using, and analyzing data from different sites. Future work can verify our ﬁndings by increasing the sample size across more sites. We postulate that, cognitively, all patients across all three sites are similar. However, there may be differences in clinical symptomatology, which informed our choice to primarily conduct experiments and analysis using data from India (i.e., Bhopal and Bangalore). The low clinical severity in terms of psychotic symptoms and lack of symptoms at the Boston site is another limitation of this paper, and why the analysis did not focus on these symptoms. While our sample was recruited from clinical populations, we did not conduct additional interviews to re-diagnose or conﬁrm the clinical diagnosis. In conclusion, our work evaluates the relationship between the traditional MCCB tests, digital cognitive assessments, and affective state for schizophrenia patients. We discovered that (1) the Rate- Correct Score shows the most utility in scoring digital cognitive assessments in a manner that renders them correlates of traditional paper-and-pencil tests; (2) of the various mindLAMP cognitive assessments, Jewels A, a mobile version of the Trails- Making Test A, has strong and signiﬁcant correlations with MCCB scores for domain-speciﬁc and overall cognition. We have highlighted the key limitations of our work and encourage future researchers to further empirically validate and advance the use of smartphone-based cognitive assessments as a tool to monitor an individual’s affective state, particularly in high-stakes applications such as schizophrenia.

METHODS The design of this study was informed by focus group discussions conducted in India and the U.S. in which participants provided feedback on their interactions with the study app, generally reporting favourably about the app and noting the importance of receiving scores to interpret their performance on the app’s cognitive assessments, prompting the current investigation into different methods of scoring digital assessments22.

Participants This multi-site 30-day observational study took place at three healthcare facilities: the Beth Israel Medical Deaconess Center

(BIDMC) in Boston, USA; the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) in Bangalore, India; and the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) and Sangath in Bhopal, India. As in prior research by this same team working with apps and psychosis18, inter-rater reliability for the PANSS was examined for research assistants administering the PANSS from each of the three sites by having them rate ﬁve video-recorded clinical interviews. Intraclass correlations were excellent (>0.75) for PANSS Total and Positive scores and fair to good (>0.4) for PANSS Negative score. Participant recruitment began in September 2024 and concluded in March 2025. Across the three sites, a total of 56 participants partook in the study; the sample demographics are summarized in Table 1. The inclusion criteria for participation in the study consisted of being at least 18 years of age, having a diagnosis schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, owning a smartphone capable of running the study app, and speaking the local language of the study site (i.e. English in the case of Boston, and English or Hindi in the case of Bhopal and Bangalore). The exclusion criteria consisted of suffering any uncontrolled mental illness or any signiﬁcant speech, sight, or hearing impairment that impacts the individual’s ability to operate a smartphone. Participants were recruited if they met the above inclusion criteria and were able to provide informed consent. The study protocol was approved by each site’s IRB, and all participants signed an informed consent prior to beginning the study. Participants met with a research assistant at the beginning of the study to complete the intake visit and again at the end of the study to complete the follow-up visit. Regular meetings were held with members of the teams across the study sites to ensure overall uniformity. At each study visit, participants completed a number of clinical assessments, such as the General Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), PANSS, Psychotic Symptom Rating Scales (PSYRATS), Calgary Depression Rating Scale for Schizophrenia (CDRSS), WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS), Social Functioning Scale (SFS), Human Connectome Project Social Task (HCP), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Phenx Access Health Services, Phenx English Proﬁciency, Phenx Health Literacy, Phenx Occupational Prestige, Phenx Social and Role Dysfunction in Psychosis and Schizophrenia, via REDCap. REDCap is a HIPAA-compliant online platform developed by Vanderbilt University that facilitates survey administration and data entry for research, supporting features such as branching logic and custom reporting53. The surveys participants completed included the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS)54.

Participants also completed the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery (MCCB)45,50, which is a gold standard assessment for measuring cognition across seven domains from verbal learning to social cognition via ten tests. During the intake study visit, the research assistant assisted participants with downloading the mindLAMP app to their phone and helped them to enable GPS permissions to allow smartphone sensor data collection; the research assistant explained to participants that they would be contacted to help with troubleshooting if their data quality proved to be low. For the 30 days of the study, participants engaged with various cognitive assessments and surveys on the mindLAMP app; on average, they were assigned 2-3 cognitive assessments and surveys per day, and received app notiﬁcations at 6 pm each day; over the course of their time in the study, participants should have completed each cognitive assessment at least 4 times. At the end of the study, participants met again with a research assistant to complete the same surveys on REDCap as at the beginning of the study, in addition to a system usability survey about their experience with the study app. Participants were compensated at the beginning and the end of the study.

Digital cognitive assessment—MindLAMP App mindLAMP is accessible in 8 languages (English, Spanish, Korean, Simpliﬁed Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Italian, French, German, and Hindi), and the app’s cognitive assessments have been codesigned with patient partners and across a series of workshops, design rounds, and ongoing app updates7,22,55. Figure 3 presents the cognitive assessments featured on the mindLAMP app: (a) Balloon Risk (Balloon Analog Risk Task), (b) Cats and Dogs (Simple Memory Task), (c) Emotion Recognition, (d) Jewels A (Trail Making Tests A), (e) Jewels B (Trail Making Tests B), (f) Maze (Problem Solving Task), (g) Pop the Bubbles (Go/No-Go Task), (h) Spatial Span, (i) Spin the Wheel (Iowa Gambling Task), and (j) Symbol Digit Substitution. Most tasks are customizable without the need for coding or changing the app. As an example, the faces used for the Emotion Recognition Task can be changed to display culturally relevant images; participants in the U.S. were presented with images taken from UPenn’s ER 40 Color Emotional Stimuli56, and participants in India were presented with images taken from the AIIMS Facial Toolbox for Emotion Recognition57. Using the smartphone data collected by the app, it is possible to generate sleep data via an algorithm that combines GPS and phone screen state: analysis will primarily concern sleep duration and sleep quality, which is roughly related to the degree of fragmentation in the data.

In-person cognitive assessment—MCCB cognitive domains For all participants, the cognitive performance was assessed via the MCCB45,50 at two time points (baseline and after 30 days). The MCCB provides scores seven cognitive domains computed from ten subtests (see Appendix A for speciﬁcs on the subtests):

1. Speed of Processing (SoP) [Trail Making Test: Part A (TMT), Brief Assessment of Cognition in Schizophrenia: Symbol Coding (BACS SC), and Category Fluency: Animal Naming (Fluency)] 2. Attention/Vigilance (AV) [Continuous Performance Test Identical Pairs (CPT-IP)] 3. Working Memory (WM) [Letter Number Span (LNS) and Wechsler Memory Scale Spatial Span (WMS III SS)] 4. Verbal Learning and Memory (Vrbl Lrng) [Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised (HVLT-R)] 5. Visual Learning and Memory (Vis Lrng) [Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised (BVMT-R)] 6. The MCCB raw scores were converted to T scores according to the U.S. English norms and corrected for age, gender, and education, and the T scores were utilized as the primary measurement for analysis. Alternate scoring. In addition to the above formulas, alternate scoring metrics informed by a review of the extant literature on cognitive assessments were implemented for speciﬁc cognitive assessments. In general, these alternate scores amount to considering either duration or accuracy exclusively: for Jewels A, Jewels B, and Maze, the amount of time to complete each level is recorded; for Emotion Recognition, Spatial Span, and Symbol Digit Substitution, the number of correct responses is recorded.

Statistical procedures All analysis was done with Python (version 3.8.8). Signiﬁcance was determined with a p-value threshold value of 0.05, and multiple comparisons were accounted for with Bonferroni corrections. Descriptive statistics were obtained for the sample’s demographics and clinical symptoms. A one-way ANOVA was performed to examine whether there were signiﬁcant differences in participant age and in MCCB scores across the three study sites. Chi-squares was performed to examine whether there were signiﬁcant differences in sex. Spearman’s correlations were calculated to assess validity between scoring metrics for mindLAMP’s digital cognitive assessments and MCCB domain scores. For these correlations, each participant’s ﬁrst available scoring metric for mindLAMP’s digital cognitive assessments was used. Test-retest reliability of the digital cognitive assessments on mindLAMP was analyzed by calculating Intraclass Correlation Coefﬁcients (ICC) for the Rate-Correct Score scoring metric for each assessment completed. To be included in this calculation, participants must have at least completed each assessment twice (this corresponded to 42 participants for Balloon Risk, 45 for Cats and Dogs, 42 for Jewels A, 41 for Jewels B, 44 for Spatial Span, 42 for Spin the Wheel, 45 for Symbol Digit Substitution, 36 for Emotion Recognition, 17 for Maze). The ICC values were computed by invoking R’s ICCest function in Python and were interpreted according to the existing guidelines in the literature60, with moderate reliability corresponding to an ICC value between 0.50 and 0.75 and high reliability corresponding to ICC values greater than 0.75. Spearman’s correlations were used to explore the relationship between sleep and performance on mindLAMP’s digital cognitive assessments. Mediation analysis was conducted using the statsmodel Python library to ﬁt a linear model using ordinary least squares to see if sleep mediated between EMA survey scores for anxiety and mood, and mindLAMP scoring metrics: the direct effect was modeled with the intraindividual z score of the EMA survey score as the predictor and the intraindividual z score of Rate-Correct Score for a particular mindLAMP assessment as the outcome; the indirect effect was modeled with the intraindividual z score of sleep duration as the mediator.

# Adolescent adversity persistently induces proinflammatory HMGB1 signaling and disrupts the basal forebrain cholinergic system in female rats

**Authors:** Hayley Ross; Makayla Adelman; Juan E Castillo; Ann Walker; Joseph Latham; Liya Qin; Victoria Macht; Fulton T Crews; Ryan P Vetreno

**Affiliations:** aBowles Center for Alcohol Studies, School of Medicine, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, 27599, USA | bDepartment of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, 27599, USA | cDepartment of Psychiatry, School of Medicine, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, 27599, USA

## Abstract

Adolescence is a critical period of neurodevelopment characterized by heightened neuroplasticity and refinement of executive functioning and cognition. Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons mature during this period, coinciding with development of adult cognitive function. Exposure to adolescent adversity has been linked to long-lasting neurobiological and cognitive consequences, yet the mechanisms underlying these outcomes remain poorly understood. Using a preclinical model of adolescent intermittent restraint stress (AIRS), we tested the hypothesis that adolescent adversity induces lasting proinflammatory innate immune signaling, loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, and cognitive deficits in adult female rats. We report that AIRS elevated plasma levels of corticosterone and proinflammatory high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), consistent with HPA axis activation and systemic inflammation. In the late adolescent (P55) basal forebrain, AIRS caused an increase of the proinflammatory signaling molecule HMGB1, the HMGB1 receptors TLR4 and RAGE, the downstream proinflammatory transcription activation marker pNF-κB p65, and proinflammatory cytokines that persisted into adulthood (P95). This was accompanied by persistent adult increases of microglial activation markers, Iba-1 and CD11b. Importantly, AIRS caused a reduction of ChAT+ and TrkA + basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that persisted into adulthood, paralleling significant impairments in recognition memory on the novel object recognition memory test. Together, these findings suggest that adolescent adversity induces persistent proinflammatory HMGB1-TLR4/RAGE-pNF-κB signaling, microglial priming, and reductions of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons as well as enduring cognitive impairment. The HMGB1 proinflammatory pathway may represent a promising therapeutic target for mitigating the long-term neurobiological and behavioral consequences of adolescent adversity.

Keywords: Adolescence, Stress, HMGB1, Neuroimmune, Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, Microglia, Cognition

## Abstract

Adolescent stress exposure elevates plasma corticosterone and HMGB1 signaling.

AIRS drives persistent HMGB1→TLR4/RAGE→NFκB neuroimmune activation

Stress primes microglia, sustaining proinflammatory states into adulthood.

AIRS reduction basal forebrain cholinergic neurons and impairs adult cognition.

HMGB1 pathway emerges as a potential target to mitigate persistent stress effects.

## Introduction

Adolescence is a conserved neurodevelopmental period characterized by substantial cognitive and neurological maturation (Spear, 2009, 2011), rendering the brain highly sensitive to environmental perturbations (McCormick et al., 2010; McCormick and Green, 2013; Crews et al., 2016, 2019; Borsini et al., 2023). Adolescence is a stressful time (Romeo, 2013), but exposure during this period to adversity, defined as uncontrollable and/or unpredictable events that threaten physical and psychological integrity, can impart long-lasting consequences on the developing brain that persist into adulthood (Spear, 2000; McCormick et al., 2010). Indeed, accumulating clinical and preclinical evidence reveals that adolescent adversity can cause changes in endocrine responsivity and neurocircuitry, increased neuroimmunity, and heightened sensitivity to later stressor exposure (Romeo et al., 2006; Andersen et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2013; Watt et al., 2017; Shaw et al., 2020; Kuhlman et al., 2023). Such adolescent adversity-related alterations are associated with subsequent development of various neuropsychiatric disorders, including depression, anxiety, and substance use disorders as well as impaired cognitive functioning, in both clinical and preclinical studies (Pine et al., 2002; Park et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; McCormick and Green, 2013). These findings underscore the need for understanding the neurobiological impacts of stress during this developmental window and identifying potential therapeutic targets that can mitigate long-term consequences.

The basal forebrain cholinergic system, the primary source of acetylcholine (ACh) innervation to the cortex, hippocampus, and other brain regions (Mesulam et al., 1983; Hecker and Mesulam, 1994; Ananth et al., 2023), is critical for cognitive functioning (Ballinger et al., 2016; Blake and Boccia, 2017). Cholinergic neurons undergo substantial refinement during adolescence (Nadler et al., 1974; Zahalka et al., 1993; Isaev et al., 2017), suggesting heightened vulnerability to stress during this developmental window. While no studies to date have investigated the effect of adolescent psychological stress on the basal forebrain cholinergic system, the existing literature reports deceased choline acetyltransferase (ChAT; the ACh-synthesizing enzyme) expression in basal forebrain cholinergic neuron target regions (e.g., prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus) of adult mice exposed to adolescent stress (Gottesfeld et al., 1978; Park et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013). Thus, the paucity of studies examining the basal forebrain cholinergic system proper, coupled with cholinergic implications in the regulation of affective balance and cognition (Chen et al., 2021; Crimmins et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024), underscores the importance of investigating the lasting effects of adolescent stress on the basal forebrain cholinergic system.

Emerging studies have increasingly implicated innate immune system activation in chronic stress-induced psychopathology, including depression, anxiety, and cognitive dysfunction that increase the risk of mental and physical illnesses (Garate et al., 2011, 2013; McEwen, 2017). While chronic stress exposure in adulthood has been reported to elicit inflammatory responses in the periphery and CNS, adolescent stress-induced changes in neuroimmune function have not been thoroughly investigated. Preclinical studies report that adult stress exposure induces proinflammatory high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) signaling pathways and downstream induction of cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα) in the hippocampus and other brain regions immediately following the conclusion of stress exposure (Frank et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022). Clinically, serum HMGB1 levels are significantly elevated in human adolescents exposed to childhood trauma that parallels onset of depressive symptomology (Xiang et al., 2025). HMGB1 is a ubiquitously expressed nuclear protein that is released following stressor exposure where it acts as an endogenous agonist at pattern recognition receptors, inducing proinflammatory neuroimmune signaling through nuclear translocation of NF-κB (Chavakis et al., 2004; Park et al., 2004; Tobon-Velasco et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Schetters et al., 2017; Andersson et al., 2018; Aucott et al., 2018). However, very few studies have investigated the lasting effects of adolescent adversity on adult innate immune activation and potential contributions to neuropathology.

In the current study, we investigated how adolescent intermittent restraint stress (AIRS), a rodent model of adolescent adversity, affects the female Wistar rat basal forebrain cholinergic system and forebrain neuroimmunity, and to determine how these neurological changes may contribute to alterations in adult cognition. Given the higher prevalence of stress-related mood and anxiety disorders in women and evidence for sex differences in stress responsivity, the present work focused on adolescent females to establish whether AIRS confers persistent basal forebrain cholinergic and cognitive pathology. We report that AIRS exposure causes lasting increases of HMGB1-mediated neuroimmune signaling and microglial activation, persistent reductions of adult female basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, and cognitive deficits in adulthood. Together, these novel findings are consistent with adolescent adversity causing lasting activation of the neuroimmune system that may contribute to the persistent loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons and impaired cognition in adult females.

## Materials and methods

### Animals

Female Wistar rats, bred and reared at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, were used in this study. On the day following birth (postnatal day [P]1), litters were maintained with their dams in standard clear plastic tubs with shavings until group housing with same-sex littermates at the time of weaning on P21. Subjects were housed in a temperature- (20 °C) and humidity-controlled vivarium on a 12/12 h light/dark cycle (light onset at 700 h) and provided ad libitum access to food and water. This study was performed in an AAALAC-accredited facility and conducted in strict accordance with NIH regulations for the care and use of animals in research. Experimental procedures reported in this study were approved by the Instructional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (Protocol: 23–124).

### Adolescent intermittent restraint stress (AIRS) paradigm

On P21, female Wistar rats (N = 46) were randomly assigned to either (i) AIRS (n = 22 [P55: n = 8, P95: n = 14]) or (ii) control (CON: n = 24 [P55: n = 8, P95: n = 16]) conditions. To minimize the impact of litter variables, no more than one subject from a given litter was assigned to a single experimental condition. The AIRS protocol was performed as previously described with modifications (Shoji and Miyakawa, 2020; Ding et al., 2021). Beginning on P25, adolescent female rats were exposed to AIRS via restraint in a tapered plastic film envelope (DecapiCone, BrainTree Scientific, Braintree, MA) for 4 h per day on a two-day on/one-day off/two-day on/two-day off intermittent schedule until P54 (Fig. 1A). The restrained rats were maintained in cages during the stress procedure in a sound-attenuated room adjacent to the housing room. Rats in the CON condition were left undisturbed in their home cages, except when monitoring body weight, cage cleaning, and behavioral testing. We utilized a chronic variable intermittent stress design to minimize habituation to repeated stress exposure (Grissom and Bhatnagar, 2009; Matovic et al., 2020). Body weights were assessed through the conclusion of experimentation and all rats evidenced dramatic body weight gains consistent with maturational development (main effect of Age: F[14,392] = 1201, p < 0.0001; Fig. 1B). However, maturational weight gains were significantly blunted in the AIRS-exposed animals (main effect of AIRS: F[1,28] = 32.9, p < 0.0001) beginning on P32 and persisting through the conclusion of experimentation.

### Plasma collection and ELISA

Tail blood was collected from CON and AIRS subjects on P25 and P54 at baseline (immediately before AIRS onset), 30 min into AIRS, and 2 h post-AIRS. Blood samples were centrifugated at 2000×g for 20 min, plasma collected, and ELISA performed for corticosterone (Enzo Life Sciences, Farmingdale, NY, Cat. #ADI-901-097) and HMGB1 (IBL International, Hamburg, Germany, Cat. #ST51011) according to the manufacturer's protocols.

### Novel Object Recognition Test (NORT)

Episodic-like memory on the NORT was assessed from P76-P78 as previously described (Vetreno and Crews, 2015; Macht et al., 2020). Briefly, the open field apparatus consists of an 80 cm × 80 cm black box. All testing was recorded and quantified using Ethovision tracking software (Ethovision XT 8.0, Noldus, Leesburg, VA). The day prior to testing, each rat was habituated to the open field apparatus and allowed to freely explore for 5 min. The open field box was cleansed with PeroxiGuard between animals to eliminate any potential olfactory cues. The testing phase occurred over two consecutive days, each with a 5 min testing duration. On the first day (familiarization phase), rats were placed in the open field box with two identical objects placed an equal distance from the subject's starting position, and the animals were allowed to freely explore the objects. Twenty-four h later, rats were returned to the open field where one of the familiar objects was replaced with a novel object (testing phase). Familiar and novel objects were counterbalanced across groups and left/right locations. In addition, all objects were previously vetted for investigative preferences. During both the familiarization and testing phases, the amount of time in contact with each object was recorded by an observer blind to condition. Investigation of objects was defined as sniffing, pawing, or having their nose oriented toward the object within a 2 cm distance. The discrimination ratio, which provides an index of novel object exploration (Bartolini et al., 1996; Antunes and Biala, 2012), was calculated by (novel object time – familiar object time)/(novel + familiar object time). The discrimination ratio varies between +1 and −1, with a positive ratio signifying more time with the novel object while a negative ratio reflects more time spent with the familiar object.

### Perfusion and brain tissue preparation

Subjects were sacrificed on either P55 (24 h post-AIRS) or P95 (40 days post-AIRS), and brain tissue collected for assessment. At the conclusion of experimentation, subjects were anesthetized with isoflurane and euthanized via thoracotomy. For immunohistochemical studies, rats from the P55 (n = 8 per group) and the P95 experiments (n = 8 for CON, n = 7 for AIRS) were transcardially perfused with 0.1 M PBS followed by 4.0 % paraformaldehyde in PBS. Brains were excised and post-fixed in 4.0 % paraformaldehyde for 24 h at 4 °C followed by 4-day fixation in a 30 % sucrose solution. Coronal sections were cut (40 μm) on a sliding microtome (MICROM HM450: ThermoScientific, Austin, TX), and sections sequentially collected into well plates and stored at −20 °C in a cryoprotectant solution (30 % glycerol/30 % ethylene glycol in PBS). For RNA extraction, P95 rats (n = 8 for CON, n = 7 for AIRS) were transcardially perfused with 0.1 M PBS, and basal forebrain tissue dissected, rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C.

### Immunohistochemistry

Free-floating tissue samples (every 6th section) containing the basal forebrain (Bregma: 1.60 mm to −2.00 mm) based on the atlas of Paxinos and Watson (2014) were washed in 0.1 M PBS, incubated in 0.6 % H2O2 to inhibit endogenous peroxidases, and blocked with normal serum (MP Biomedicals, Solon, OH). Sections were incubated in a primary antibody solution for 48 h at 4 °C. Primary antibodies, dilutions, and validation information are included in Table 1. Sections were washed with PBS, incubated for 1 h in a biotinylated secondary antibody (Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA), and incubated for 1 h in avidin-biotin complex solution (Vectastain ABC Kit: Vector Laboratories). The chromogen, nickel-enhanced diaminobenzidine (Sigma-Aldrich, Burlington, Massachusetts), was used to visualize immunoreactivity. Tissue were mounted onto slides, dehydrated, and cover slipped. Negative control for non-specific binding was conducted on separate sections employing the above procedures but omitting the primary antibody.

### Microscopic quantification and image analysis

Across experiments, BioQuant Nova Advanced Image Analysis software (R&M Biometric, Nashville, TN) was used for image capture and quantification of IHC. Representative images were captured using an Olympus BX50 microscope and Sony DXC-390 video camera linked to a computer. For each measure, the microscope, camera, and software were background corrected and normalized to preset light levels to ensure fidelity of data acquisition. A modified unbiased stereological quantification method was used, which was performed by experimenters blind to treatment, to quantify ChAT + IR, TrkA + IR, HMGB1+IR, TLR4+IR, RAGE + IR, and pNF-κBp65+IR cells in the basal forebrain. We previously reported that comparison of traditional unbiased stereological methodology with our modified unbiased stereological approach yielded nearly identical values for heterogeneously distributed cell populations (Crews et al., 2004). The outlined regions of interest were determined and data expressed as cells/mm2. For quantification of cholinergic neurons across subregions of the adult (i.e., P95) basal forebrain, ChAT+ was assessed in the medial septum (MS; Bregma: 1.60 mm–0.00 mm), vertical limb of the diagonal band (VDB; Bregma: 1.60 mm–0.48 mm), horizontal limb of the diagonal band (HDB; Bregma: 1.08 mm to −1.56 mm), substantia innominata (SI; Bregma: 0.96 mm to −0.84 mm), and nucleus basalis magnocellularis (NBM; Bregma: 0.36 mm to −2.00 mm) as depicted in Supplemental Fig. 1. Expression of CD11b + IR and Iba-1+IR microglia were assessed in the basal forebrain using pixel density, and data expressed as × 1000 pixels/mm2.

### RNA isolation and reverse transcription PCR (RTPCR)

Total RNA was extracted from dissected basal forebrain tissue samples from CON and AIRS subjects sacrificed on P95 by homogenization in TRI reagent (Sigma-Aldrich) following the single-step method of RNA isolation (Chomczynski and Sacchi, 2006). RNA quality and concentration were determined using a Qubit Fluorometer (Qubit™ 4 Fluorometer; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) in combination with a Qubit™ RNA Broad Range Assay kit (Invitrogen). Total RNA was reverse transcribed as previously described (Vetreno et al., 2018; Fisher et al., 2025). RTPCR was run on a Bio-Rad CFX system (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA) using SYBER Green PCR Master Mix (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA). RTPCR was run with an initial activation for 10 min at 95 °C, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation (95 °C, 15 s), annealing/extension (57–58 °C, 1 min), and melt curve. The primer sequences are presented in Table 2. Differences in primer expression between groups are expressed as cycle time (Ct) values normalized with housekeeping genes, and relative differences between groups are calculated and expressed as the percent difference relative to CONs.

### Statistical analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS (IBM; Chicago, IL) and GraphPad Software (Prism 10; San Diego, CA). Body weight and plasma ELISAs were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVAs with post-hoc Bonferroni corrections performed as necessary and described in the Results section. IHC data comparing CON and AIRS groups across ages were analyzed using 2 × 2 ANOVAs with post-hoc Bonferroni corrections or Šidák's MCT performed as necessary and described in the Results section. RTPCR data and IHC data at individual ages as well as NORT behavioral data were analyzed using two-tailed Student's t tests. Levene's test for equality of variance was performed for each analysis. When reported in the Results, Welch's t tests were used to assess data with unequal variances. Two-tailed Pearson's r were used for all correlative analyses. All values are reported as mean ± SEM, and significance was defined as p < 0.05.

## Results

### Adolescent intermittent restraint stress persistently induces plasma stress markers as well as neuroimmune and microglial activation markers in the basal forebrain of late adolescent rats that persist into adulthood

Assessment of plasma corticosterone levels, which provides an index of HPA axis activation in response to stress, revealed that AIRS significantly increased plasma corticosterone levels 30 min into the stress exposure on both P25 (p < 0.0001, Bonferroni) and P54 (p < 0.0001, Bonferroni), which returned to baseline levels 2 h following the conclusion of AIRS exposure (both p's < 0.0001, Bonferroni; Fig. 2A). We observed higher baseline corticosterone plasma levels at P25 compared to P54 (main effect of Age: F[1,13] = 13.4, p = 0.003) that was likely driven by movement of animals to the testing room. As glucocorticoids have been reported to prime immune responses to subsequent immune challenges and corticosterone increases HMGB1 expression (Frank et al., 2016, 2019; Fu et al., 2019), we next assessed plasma HMGB1 levels during AIRS exposure. At initiation of AIRS exposure on P25, plasma HMGB1 levels did not change at baseline or 30 min into AIRS, but was increased approximately 1.8-fold 2 h following the conclusion of AIRS exposure (p = 0.006, Bonferroni; Fig. 2B). At the conclusion of AIRS on P54, plasma levels of HMGB1 were increased approximately 1.7-fold 30 min into AIRS exposure relative to age-matched CONs (p = 0.0006, Bonferroni; Fig. 2C). Thus, AIRS increases plasma corticosterone and HMGB1 levels.

Given our findings of AIRS-induced alterations in plasma HMGB1 levels, we next investigated HMGB1 expression in the basal forebrain immediately following the conclusion of AIRS exposure (i.e., P55) and 40 days following the conclusion (i.e., P95). Quantification of basal forebrain HMGB1+IR revealed an age-associated increase, regardless of stress exposure (main effect of Age: F[1,25] = 464.9, p < 0.0001). Further, AIRS caused a persistent increase of HMGB1+IR in the basal forebrain, relative to age-matched CONs (main effect of AIRS: F[1,25] = 100.9, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3A). HMGB1 is a nuclear protein that when released acts as an endogenous proinflammatory neuroimmune ligand at pattern recognition receptors including TLR4 and RAGE. Immunohistological assessment of basal forebrain TLR4 (main effect of Age: F[1,27] = 96.8, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3B) and RAGE (main effect of Age: F[1,28] = 69.3, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3C) expression revealed an age-associated reduction, regardless of stress exposure. Post-hoc assessment revealed that AIRS increased TLR4+IR by approximately 1.4-fold in the late adolescent basal forebrain (p < 0.0001, Bonferroni) which remained elevated approximately 1.3-fold into adulthood (p = 0.036, Bonferroni). Assessment of RAGE expression revealed an overall AIRS-induced increase relative to age-matched CONs (main effect of AIRS: F[1,28] = 33.6, p < 0.0001). HMGB1 binds to, activates, and induces TLR4, RAGE, and other receptors, leading to activation and nuclear translocation of NF-κB, a key proinflammatory transcription factor involved in induction of proinflammatory cytokines (Mayfield et al., 2013; Crews et al., 2017). Quantification of activated pNF-κB p65+IR revealed an age-associated increase in the basal forebrain (main effect of Age: F[1,28] = 314.8, p < 0.0001). Post-hoc analysis revealed that AIRS increased pNF-κB p65+IR by approximately 1.2-fold on P55 (p = 0.028, Bonferroni) and 1.4-fold on P95 (p < 0.0001, Bonferroni; Fig. 3D). Assessment of proinflammatory cytokine mRNA in the adult (i.e., P95) basal forebrain revealed a 1.6-fold increase of Il1β (t[12] = 2.8, p = 0.015, Student's t-test) and a 1.7-fold increase of Tnfα (t[12] = 2.9, p = 0.015, Student's t-test) relative to age-matched CONs (Fig. 3E). mRNA levels of Ccl2 and Il6 were unchanged. These data are consistent with our hypothesis that adolescent adversity increases HMGB1-mediated proinflammatory neuroimmune signaling cascades in the late adolescent basal forebrain that persist into adulthood.

To determine if AIRS causes long-term alterations in basal forebrain microglia, the resident immune effector cells of CNS, we assessed expression of the pan-microglial marker Iba-1 and CD11b, which is a constitutively-expressed microglial-specific marker upregulated in activated microglia (Kettenmann et al., 2013). Immunohistological assessment of Iba-1+ microglia in late adolescence (i.e., P55) revealed an approximate 1.8-fold increase (t[14] = 10.0, p < 0.0001, Student's t-test; Fig. 4A) and a 1.3-fold increase of Iba1 mRNA in the adult (i.e., P95) basal forebrain (t[12] = 2.9, p = 0.014, Student's t-test; Fig. 4B). Quantification of CD11b + IR revealed an age-associated increase in the basal forebrain (main effect of Age: F[1,27] = 33.2, p < 0.0001). Further, AIRS increased CD11b + IR approximately 2.0-fold immediately following the conclusion of AIRS, an effect that persisted into adulthood (main effect of AIRS: F[1,27] = 46.6, p < 0.0001; Fig. 4C). These data reveal that AIRS exposure shifts microglia to an activated state that persists into adulthood. Taken together, these data are consistent with adolescent adversity inducing proinflammatory HMGB1-TLR4/RAGE-pNF-κB p65 signaling and microglial activation in the adolescent basal forebrain that persists into adulthood that may contribute to developmental alterations in neurobiology.

### Adolescent intermittent restraint stress decreases basal forebrain cholinergic neuron markers in late adolescence that persists into adulthood

Generated early in embryonic development (Gould et al., 1989, 1991; Dinopoulos et al., 1992; Linke and Frotscher, 1993), cholinergic neurons continue to undergo maturational refinement and consolidation of projections and receptors during adolescence (Matthews et al., 1974; Nadler et al., 1974; Zahalka et al., 1993), increasing their vulnerability to neuroimmune and developmental insults. To investigate whether AIRS alters basal forebrain cholinergic neuron populations, we first quantified immunohistochemical expression of the ACh-synthesizing enzyme ChAT, which revealed an approximate overall 31 % reduction in late adolescence that persisted into adulthood (main effect of AIRS: F[1,28] = 17.3, p = 0.0003; Fig. 5A/B). Moreover, ChAT + cholinergic neurons across subregions of the basal forebrain provide vast cortical and limbic projections, and AIRS caused a lasting reduction of ChAT + neurons across the rostral-caudal extent of the basal forebrain (Supplemental Fig. 1). TrkA, the high-affinity nerve growth factor receptor, is a cholinergic neuron marker (Vetreno et al., 2020) critical for the survival and maintenance of the cholinergic neuron phenotype. Assessment of TrkA + IR revealed an approximate 30 % reduction in the late adolescent basal forebrain, an effect that persisted into adulthood (main effect of AIRS: F[1,26] = 20.2, p = 0.0001; Fig. 5C). These data are consistent with adolescent adversity causing reductions of basal forebrain cholinergic neuron populations that persist into adulthood.

Given our previous findings that HMGB1-mediated neuroimmune activation contributes to reductions in basal forebrain cholinergic neuron populations (Crews and Vetreno, 2022; Crews et al., 2023), we next correlated expression of HMGB1-TLR4/RAGE-pNF-κB p65 neuroimmune signaling molecules and the microglial activation marker CD11b with the cholinergic neuron marker ChAT in the adult basal forebrain. Immunohistological expression of ChAT + cholinergic neurons was negatively correlated with HMGB1+IR (r = −0.77, p = 0.0005, Pearson's r), RAGE + IR (r = −0.64, p = 0.007, Pearson's r), pNF-κB p65+IR (r = −0.78, p = 0.0003, Pearson's r), and CD11b + IR (r = −0.62, p = 0.013, Pearson's r). These data suggest that AIRS induction of HMGB1-TLR4/RAGE-pNF-κB p65 neuroimmune signaling and microglial activation may contribute to loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons.

### Adolescent intermittent restraint stress confers lasting novel object recognition memory impairments in adulthood

Given that the cholinergic system is crucial for cognitive functioning and our discovery that AIRS causes a lasting reduction of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, we next assessed novel object recognition memory in adulthood following AIRS exposure. Adolescent intermittent restraint stress did not affect time in contact with the objects or distance traveled during the familiarization phase of the NORT (all p's > 0.07). During the testing phase, AIRS did not affect distance traveled (p = 0.50, Fig. 6A) but did significantly reduce the discrimination ratio in adulthood, relative to CONs (t[3.7] = 9.4, p = 0.004, Welch's t-test; Fig. 6B). We next correlated basal forebrain cholinergic neuron marker expression with the discrimination index on the novel object recognition memory test. The discrimination index was positively correlated with expression of both ChAT (r = 0.52, p = 0.045, Pearson's r) and TrkA (r = 0.58, p = 0.024, Pearson's r; Fig. 6C). Thus, AIRS exposure causes a lasting impairment in adult object recognition memory that may be related to persistent reductions of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons.

## Discussion

To our knowledge, this is the first study to report that adolescent intermittent restraint stress (AIRS), a preclinical model of human adolescent adversity, causes proinflammatory innate immune system activation and reduction of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons in the late adolescent (i.e., P55) basal forebrain that persists into adulthood (i.e., P95), paralleling adult cognitive deficits in adult female rats. Specifically, we discovered that AIRS robustly elevated plasma levels of the stress hormone corticosterone during stress exposure, confirming activation of the HPA axis, and increased circulating HMGB1 both during and following the stress exposure, suggesting activation of systemic proinflammatory signaling cascades. These peripheral responses were paralleled by a significant upregulation of HMGB1 expression in the basal forebrain immediately following the conclusion of AIRS (P55) that remained elevated 40 days after stress cessation indicating that adolescent stress triggers long-lasting neuroimmune activation. Consistent with AIRS-induced upregulation of HMGB1 was our observation of concomitant increased expression of the HMGB1 receptors TLR4 and RAGE as well as the downstream proinflammatory nuclear transcription factor phosphorylated (activated) NF-κB p65 that together support an AIRS-induced sustained proinflammatory transcriptional state in the adult basal forebrain. This neuroimmune activation was accompanied by a lasting shift in microglial phenotype, evidenced by increased Iba-1 and CD11b expression, consistent with persistent microglial activation or priming. Importantly, we found that AIRS caused a ∼30 % reduction in basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, as indexed by reductions of ChAT and TrkA immunoreactivity, which persisted into adulthood. Correlational analyses suggest that reductions of ChAT + neurons were strongly and inversely associated with HMGB1, RAGE, pNF-κB p65, and CD11b expression, supporting a mechanistic link between AIRS-induced proinflammatory HMGB1-mediated neuroimmune activation and cholinergic neuron vulnerability (Vetreno and Crews, 2018; Vetreno et al., 2020; Crews et al., 2021; Crews and Vetreno, 2022). These neurobiological changes were accompanied by significant impairments in adult recognition memory as indicated by a reduced discrimination index on the novel object recognition test, which positively correlated with cholinergic marker expression. Together, these findings suggest that adolescent adversity in females establishes a long-lasting proinflammatory neuroimmune environment in the basal forebrain in association with a persistent reduction in cholinergic neuron populations, leading to cognitive deficits in adulthood.

Our findings extend the literature on stress-induced neuroimmune activation by revealing that adolescent adversity leads to persistent induction of the proinflammatory HMGB1-TLR4/RAGE-pNF-κB signaling axis in the female basal forebrain, a region critically involved in cognition and affect regulation. While previous studies have shown that chronic stress in adulthood increases HMGB1 expression and proinflammatory cytokine production in the hippocampus and other limbic structures (Frank et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022), few studies have examined whether these responses endure after stress termination—particularly when the stressor is experienced during adolescence. Here, we show that elevations in basal forebrain HMGB1 as well as the HMGB1 receptors TLR4 and RAGE remain detectable 40 days after AIRS exposure, suggesting that adolescent adversity induces persistent, long-lasting neuroimmune signaling in this region (Qin et al., 2007). This is consistent with the concept of microglial priming, wherein early-life immune challenges shift microglia toward a hyper-responsive phenotype that can perpetuate low-grade inflammation or exaggerated responses to subsequent insults (Bilbo and Schwarz, 2009; Melbourne et al., 2021). The observed increases in Iba-1 and CD11b, both immediately following the conclusion of AIRS (P55) and well into adulthood (P95), long after cessation of stressor exposure, further support the hypothesis of a chronically activated or sensitized microglial population. Such sustained neuroimmune activation may disrupt the microenvironment of the basal forebrain that promotes cholinergic neuron vulnerability through increased cytokine production, oxidative stress, and epigenetic repression of cholinergic phenotype genes, as we and others have reported in models of adolescent alcohol exposure (Crews and Vetreno, 2022; Crews et al., 2023; Fecik et al., 2024). Moreover, these findings suggest that the cholinergic-rich basal forebrain may be uniquely vulnerable to innate immune induction following AIRS, as other studies employing adolescent mixed modality stress do not show lasting neuroimmune induction in other brain regions, such as the hippocampus, in the absence of a secondary challenge (Pyter et al., 2013). Taken together, these results position HMGB1-mediated neuroimmune signaling as a central mechanistic link between adolescent adversity and lasting alterations in basal forebrain neurobiology.

Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons are generated prenatally but undergo maturational refinement during adolescence, including consolidation of cortical and hippocampal projections and trophic factor signaling (Matthews et al., 1974; Zahalka et al., 1993; Isaev et al., 2017), which may render them especially vulnerable to neuroimmune insults during this developmental window. We report that adolescent adversity causes a persistent reduction of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, as indexed by decreased ChAT and TrkA immunoreactivity that endures well into adulthood. Prior studies have reported that adolescent social defeat stress reduces ChAT expression in basal forebrain cholinergic neuron target regions (Huang et al., 2013) and that adult stressors diminish cholinergic tone in the hippocampus (Gottesfeld et al., 1978; Park et al., 2010); however, the current study is, to our knowledge, the first to directly demonstrate cholinergic neuron loss across the rostral-caudal extent of the adult basal forebrain following adolescent stress exposure. The strong negative correlations we observed between ChAT expression and HMGB1, RAGE, pNF-κB p65, and CD11b suggest that neuroimmune activation is not merely coincident but may be causally related to cholinergic phenotype suppression. These findings align with recent work showing that HMGB1-TLR4 signaling drives REST-G9a-mediated epigenetic repression of cholinergic genes (Vetreno et al., 2020; Crews et al., 2021, 2023; Crews and Vetreno, 2022), providing a possible mechanistic link between AIRS-induced neuroimmune activation and long-term cholinergic deficits. Functionally, we observed that AIRS-exposed animals exhibited a significant reduction in novel object recognition memory, a cognitive domain critically dependent on cholinergic input from the caudal basal forebrain to the perirhinal cortex and hippocampus (Bartolini et al., 1996; Antunes and Biala, 2012). The positive correlations between ChAT/TrkA expression and discrimination ratio on the novel object recognition memory test further strengthen the interpretation that loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons may contribute to the observed cognitive impairments observed in adult AIRS-treated rats. Together, these results underscore the importance of maintaining basal forebrain cholinergic integrity during adolescence and suggest that proinflammatory neuroimmune signaling pathways may be tractable therapeutic targets to prevent or reverse stress-related cognitive decline.

Collectively, these findings suggest adolescence as a critical window of vulnerability in which adversity can produce enduring neuroimmune and neurotransmitter system alterations with long-term consequences for cognitive function. The persistence of HMGB1-TLR4/RAGE-pNF-κB signaling and microglial activation observed in the current study suggests that adolescent adversity may induce a lasting neuroimmune signature that could contribute to the pathophysiology of stress-related psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Indeed, human studies demonstrate that individuals with a history of early-life adversity exhibit elevated circulating HMGB1 and proinflammatory cytokines, heightened HPA axis responsivity, and increased risk for depression, anxiety, and substance use disorders (Kuhlman et al., 2023; Xiang et al., 2025). Our findings also resonate with evidence that cholinergic hypofunction is a common feature of Alzheimer's disease, age-related cognitive decline, and stress-related disorders (Paul et al., 2015; Ballinger et al., 2016), suggesting that adolescent adversity may accelerate or predispose individuals to these conditions via premature loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons. Importantly, our observation that proinflammatory neuroimmune, microglial, and cholinergic alterations persist for more than a month after stressor cessation identifies potential targets for intervention. Future studies should evaluate whether pharmacological blockade of HMGB1 or its receptors (e.g., TLR4 antagonists, RAGE inhibitors), microglial modulators such as minocycline, or pro-cholinergic strategies (e.g., acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, neurotrophic factor agonists, DREADD-based stimulation) can prevent or reverse AIRS-induced reductions of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons and cognitive deficits in adulthood. Moreover, given that microglial phenotypes are dynamic and potentially reversible, interventions administered after stress exposure may restore homeostasis and rescue cognitive function. Together, these results underscore the translational significance of targeting neuroimmune signaling pathways and cholinergic systems as promising strategies to mitigate the long-term impact of adolescent adversity on brain health.

While the findings of the current study are compelling, several limitations warrant consideration. First, the goal of the present study was to establish the persistent effects of AIRS exposure on the innate immune and the basal forebrain cholinergic system in adulthood. Although these initial studies solely utilized females given the higher prevalence of mood disorder diagnosis in female humans, future studies will determine if sex-specific adolescent vulnerabilities emerge following AIRS exposure. Second, while this study reveals that AIRS exposure confers lasting basal forebrain cholinergic system pathology, our lack of an adult comparison group limits our ability to conclude that adolescence is a unique sensitive window for stress-induced neurological disruption. Future studies will therefore compare intermittent restraint stress responsivity between adolescent and adult rats across neuroimmune, cholinergic, and behavioral outcomes. Third, although we report that AIRS causes a persistent reduction in basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, the present study did not assess the impact of AIRS on cholinergic projections and synaptic integrity in target regions (e.g., prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, amygdala) or the contribution of altered ACh tone to behavioral impairments in adulthood. Future studies will combine synaptic markers and in vivo measures of cholinergic signaling in cortical and limbic targets to more precisely define the circuit and synaptic mechanisms linking AIRS to long-lasting cognitive and affective dysfunction. Finally, we did not monitor estrous cycle stage, and animals were not euthanized at a defined phase of the cycle. Given that ovarian hormones can modulate basal forebrain cholinergic Chat mRNA expression and function (Luine, 1985; Gibbs, 1998), future studies should determine whether AIRS interacts with estrous phase of ovarian hormone status to influence the magnitude and persistence of basal forebrain cholinergic neuron deficits and cognitive dysfunction in adulthood.

In summary, our study establishes that AIRS elicits enduring neuroimmune activation, disrupts basal forebrain cholinergic neuron populations, and impairs adult cognition. These findings underscore the importance of adolescence as a sensitive neurodevelopmental window during which stress can produce long-lasting alterations in brain circuits that regulate cognition and behavior, and identify the HMGB1-TLR4/RAGE-pNF-κB axis as a promising therapeutic target for mitigating the long-term consequences of adolescent adversity.

## Abstract

When recalling autobiographical events, people retrieve not only the event details, but also the

feelings they experienced. Past work with different measures of memories for feelings remain

inconclusive, suggesting that people are either highly consistent or inconsistent with

remembering feelings. The current study examined whether people are able to consistently recall

the intensity of previous feelings associated with consequential and negatively valenced

emotional events, i.e., the 9/11 attack (N = 769) and Covid-19 pandemic (N = 726). By

comparing the initial and recalled intensities of negative feelings, we found that people

systematically recall more intense negative feelings than they initially reported – overestimating

the intensity of past negative emotional experience. The Covid-19 dataset further showed that

people whose emotional well-being improved more demonstrate smaller biases in remembered

feelings. Across both datasets, the remembered intensity of feelings correlated with initial

feelings and were also influenced by current feelings, although the impact of the current feelings

was stronger in the Covid-19 dataset than the 9/11 dataset. Our results suggest that when

recalling negative autobiographical events, people tend to overestimate the intensity of

experienced negative emotional experience with the degree of bias influenced by current feelings

and well-being.

Keywords: Memory, Emotion, Appraisal, Autobiographical memory, Well-being
